::: {.gw-lede}
Most engineering calculators give you a number and nothing else — no equation, no
source, and no warning when you have pushed a formula past the range it was
derived for. Darcy's law quietly stops describing reality above a pore Reynolds
number of about 1, and nothing on the web tells you when you have crossed it.
These tools do.

Nothing is uploaded. Every calculation runs in your browser.
:::

## All tools

::: {#all-tools}
:::

## Why another calculator

::: {.gw-lede}
Three things are different here, and each of them exists because getting them
wrong is common in practice.

**Every tool states where it stops working.** A formula has a domain of validity,
and outside it the answer is not merely imprecise — it is wrong. The Darcy
calculator computes a pore Reynolds number and tells you which regime you are in.
The Theis calculator reports whether the Cooper–Jacob approximation may be used at
your radius and time. Tools that follow will do the same for their own limits.

**Every equation is sourced.** Not "as found in the literature", but the actual
paper or textbook, with the table number where a reference value came from. You
should be able to check the work.

**Quantities that are easy to confuse are shown side by side.** Darcy flux and
seepage velocity differ by a factor of 1/*n*; using one where the other belongs
is the most frequent error in contaminant travel-time work. Both appear in the
output, always.
:::

## The articles behind the tools

::: {.gw-lede}
These calculators are the working end of the writing on this site. The
[Groundwater Science series](/blog-en) derives the equations and then solves the
same problems numerically with MODFLOW, FloPy and PHREEQC — the pumping test the
Theis calculator evaluates at a point is fitted to a full drawdown curve in the
series, and the water analysis this charge-balance tool validates is the input a
speciation run begins with.
:::
